title: Is Speculative Decoding Worth It? Profiling vLLM on NVIDIA Blackwell — Akamai
talk_summary: A single-GPU vLLM profiling demo of speculative decoding on Blackwell, showing ~1.6x faster generation on structured output (high draft acceptance) versus poor gains on creative/high-temperature tasks and long-context workloads where prefill dominates. The practical message is a decision checklist: only enable when you have spare VRAM, low concurrency, short outputs, and structured tasks.

takeaways.technique: Speculative decoding only for structured, short-output, low-concurrency calls
takeaways.what_they_do: Run a small draft model (10-50x smaller, same tokenizer/family) to propose 3-5 tokens per cycle; the target model verifies them in one forward pass, so output quality is unchanged but generation is faster when acceptance is high.
takeaways.evidence_quote: with a speculative on the right side um it was able to generate much much faster um 1.6 times faster
takeaways.numbers: ~1.6x faster generation on structured output; draft model 2.5GB vs 16GB baseline weights

takeaways.technique: Match decoding optimization to task structure and output/input ratio
takeaways.what_they_do: They classify workloads: structured (code, JSON, SQL) benefit; creative/high-temperature and long-context/RAG with short outputs do not, because prefill dominates and acceptance rate is low.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it helps with some use cases when you have a workload that is more like highly structured like coding use cases

takeaways.technique: Prefill vs decode cost split as a routing heuristic
takeaways.what_they_do: They note speculative decoding accelerates only token generation, not prompt reading/KV-cache building, so long-context RAG or document analysis with short outputs sees little benefit.
takeaways.evidence_quote: with speculative decoding it's supposed to accelerate the generating part not the part where the model reads the prompt
